title: CUET Political Science Test 3
subject: Political Science (Code: 323)
syllabus_source: CUET SYLLABUS/Political Science - 323.pdf (NTA syllabus for CUET (UG) 2026, latest published)

One set of 5 questions is based on a passage; the set stays together.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: Which is NOT a pillar of the ASEAN Community
questions.question: The ASEAN Community is built on three pillars. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The ASEAN Monetary Union
Why: The ASEAN Community has three pillars: security, economic, and socio-cultural. ASEAN has no monetary union or single currency.
Why not the others: (A), (B), (C) are the three pillars of the ASEAN Community.
Key point: ASEAN integrates without a common currency, unlike the Euro area.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Recent Issues and Challenges
questions.sub_topic: Court order of 1986 on the Ayodhya site
questions.question: In February 1986, what did the Faizabad district court order regarding the disputed site at Ayodhya?
options: A) The site was to be handed over to the Archaeological Survey.
B) The premises were to be unlocked so that people could worship there.
C) A mosque was to be built at a new location.
D) All religious activity at the site was banned.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The premises were to be unlocked so that people could worship there.
Why: In February 1986 the court ordered the premises to be unlocked. This set off mobilisation on both sides and deepened the dispute.
Why not the others:
(A) No such handover was ordered in 1986.
(C) No such order was made by the district court.
(D) The order opened, rather than closed, the site.
Key point: The 1986 order was a turning point in the Ayodhya dispute.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: Party Jagjivan Ram formed before the 1977 election
questions.question: Just before the 1977 election, Jagjivan Ram left the Congress and formed a new party, which joined the Janata alliance. It was called the:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Congress for Democracy
Why: Jagjivan Ram formed the Congress for Democracy, which later merged into the Janata Party.
Why not the others:
(A) The Lok Dal was Charan Singh's later party.
(B) The Congress (O) came from the 1969 split.
(D) The Bharatiya Kranti Dal was Charan Singh's party of the 1960s.
Key point: Defections from the Congress strengthened the Janata alliance in 1977.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: When India ratified the Kyoto Protocol
questions.question: In which year did India sign and ratify the 1997 Kyoto Protocol?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 2002
Why: India signed and ratified the Kyoto Protocol in August 2002. As a developing country, it was exempt from binding targets.
Why not the others:
(A) 1992 was the Earth Summit.
(B) 1997 was when the Protocol was agreed.
(C) 2005 is when the Protocol came into force.
Key point: India joined Kyoto but stresses differentiated responsibilities.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: European and Asian regional bodies in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) Euro notes and coins introduced in twelve member states
(B) Formation of the European Economic Community
(C) Signing of the Maastricht Treaty
(D) Formation of ASEAN
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (B), (D), (C), (A)
Why: (B) The EEC was formed in 1957. (D) ASEAN was set up in 1967. (C) The Maastricht Treaty was signed in 1992. (A) Euro notes and coins came into use in January 2002.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts Maastricht before ASEAN. Option (B) puts ASEAN before the EEC. Option (D) puts the Euro before Maastricht.
Key point: 1957 → 1967 → 1992 → 2002.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: International bodies in order of founding
questions.question:
Arrange the following international bodies in the order of their founding:
(A) World Trade Organisation
(B) United Nations
(C) International Atomic Energy Agency
(D) League of Nations
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (D), (B), (C), (A)
Why: (D) The League of Nations was set up after the First World War, in 1919–20. (B) The UN was founded in 1945. (C) The IAEA was set up in 1957. (A) The WTO came in 1995.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts the UN before the League. Option (C) puts the IAEA before the UN. Option (D) puts the WTO before the IAEA.
Key point: The UN replaced the League, which failed to prevent a second world war.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: What led to the formation of the Mizo National Front
questions.question: The Mizo National Front was formed in 1961 after anger at the Assam government's failure to respond adequately to:
options: A) the great famine of 1959 in the Mizo hills
B) the war of 1962 with China in the north-east
C) the Partition of Bengal and its aftermath
D) the anti-Hindi language riots of 1965
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) the great famine of 1959 in the Mizo hills
Why: The great famine of 1959 in the Mizo hills, and the Assam government's poor response, led to the formation of the MNF under Laldenga.
Why not the others:
(B) The MNF was formed before the 1962 war.
(C) The Partition of Bengal was in 1905.
(D) The language riots were in Tamil Nadu.
Key point: Neglect turned grievance into a secessionist movement.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: Leader who was NOT a founder of the Non-Aligned Movement
questions.question: Which of the following leaders was NOT one of the founding leaders of the Non-Aligned Movement?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Zhou Enlai
Why: Zhou Enlai, China's Premier, attended Bandung but was not a founder of NAM. Its founders included Nehru, Tito of Yugoslavia, Nasser of Egypt, Sukarno of Indonesia and Nkrumah of Ghana.
Why not the others: (A) Tito, (B) Nasser and (C) Sukarno were founding leaders of NAM.
Key point: NAM was led by newly independent and non-bloc states.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: India's nuclear doctrine on first use
questions.question: India's nuclear doctrine, adopted after the 1998 tests, commits India to:
options: A) using nuclear weapons first in any war
B) no first use of nuclear weapons
C) giving up its nuclear weapons by 2000
D) signing the NPT as a nuclear-weapon state
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) no first use of nuclear weapons
Why: India's doctrine is credible minimum deterrence and "no first use". It will not use nuclear weapons first but will retaliate if attacked.
Why not the others:
(A) That is the opposite of the doctrine.
(C) India did not commit to giving up its weapons.
(D) The NPT recognises only five nuclear-weapon states; India has not signed it.
Key point: No first use and minimum deterrence define India's doctrine.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: What cooperative security involves
questions.question: Cooperative security in the non-traditional view relies on:
options: A) the military alliances led by a single superpower
B) the use of force by individual states acting alone
D) cooperation among states, global bodies and NGOs
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) cooperation among states, global bodies and NGOs
Why: Non-traditional threats cross borders and need cooperative responses involving states, international organisations, NGOs, businesses and other actors.
Why not the others:
(A) Alliances of one power are a traditional approach.
(B) Unilateral force is a traditional approach.
(C) Withdrawing would weaken cooperation.
Key point: Problems that cross borders need cooperation that crosses them.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: Early party-system milestones in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) Formation of the Swatantra Party
(B) Setting up of the Election Commission of India
(C) The third general election
(D) Formation of the Bharatiya Jana Sangh
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (B), (D), (A), (C)
Why: (B) The Election Commission was set up in January 1950. (D) The Jana Sangh was formed in 1951. (A) The Swatantra Party was formed in 1959. (C) The third general election was held in 1962.
Why not the others: Option (B) puts the Jana Sangh before the Commission. Option (C) puts Swatantra before the Jana Sangh. Option (D) puts the 1962 election before Swatantra.
Key point: 1950 → 1951 → 1959 → 1962.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: Punjab in the 1980s — the false claim
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Indira Gandhi was assassinated on 31 October 1984.
(B) Her assassination was followed by violence against the Sikh community in Delhi and other places.
(C) The Akali Dal led the movement for a Punjabi-speaking State.
(D) The Rajiv Gandhi–Longowal Accord ended militancy in Punjab immediately.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (D) only
Why: Only (D) is false: violence continued for about a decade after the 1985 Accord, until peace returned in the mid-1990s.
Why not the others: (A) Indira Gandhi was killed by her bodyguards on 31 October 1984. (B) anti-Sikh violence followed in Delhi and elsewhere. (C) the Akali Dal led the Punjabi Suba movement. Options (A), (B) and (C) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Accords open a path to peace but do not end conflict at once.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: Lal Bahadur Shastri's famous slogan
questions.question: Which slogan did Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri give during the 1965 war and the food crisis?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Jai Jawan Jai Kisan
Why: Shastri's 'Jai Jawan Jai Kisan' honoured soldiers and farmers, symbolising the two challenges of war and food shortage.
Why not the others:
(B) 'Garibi Hatao' was Indira Gandhi's 1971 slogan.
(C) 'Inquilab Zindabad' dates from the freedom struggle.
(D) 'Aaram Haram Hai' (rest is forbidden) was Nehru's call to work.
Key point: Shastri led India through the 1965 war and food crisis.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Democratic Upsurge and Coalition Politics
questions.sub_topic: New parties and the end of one-party rule — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The Bharatiya Janata Party was formed in 1980.
(B) The Janata Dal was formed in 1988.
(C) No party won a clear majority in the 1989 Lok Sabha election.
(D) The BJP formed the government at the Centre after the 1991 election.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) the BJP was formed in 1980 by former Jana Sangh members. (B) the Janata Dal was formed in 1988. (C) the 1989 election produced a hung Parliament.
Why not the others: (D) is false: after the 1991 election the Congress formed a minority government under P.V. Narasimha Rao. Options (C) and (D) include (D); option (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: 1989 began the era of hung Parliaments.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Politics of Planned Development
questions.sub_topic: A political effect of the Green Revolution
questions.question: One political effect of the Green Revolution, according to NCERT, was:
options: A) the end of all regional inequality in Indian farming
B) the abolition of the zamindari system across India
C) the nationalisation of all of the country's farm land
D) the rise of middle peasants as a political force
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) the rise of middle peasants as a political force
Why: Farmers with medium-sized holdings gained most from the new technology. These middle peasants became politically influential in many parts of India.
Why not the others:
(A) The Green Revolution widened regional and class differences.
(B) Zamindari abolition came earlier, through land reform.
(C) Land was never nationalised.
Key point: The Green Revolution raised output and the political weight of middle peasants.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: Phrase for South Korea's rapid growth
questions.question: South Korea's rapid economic growth from the 1960s to the 1980s is often called:
options: A) the Asian Tiger miracle of the Yangtze
C) the 'Miracle on the Han River'
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) the 'Miracle on the Han River'
Why: South Korea's transformation is known as the 'Miracle on the Han River', after the river that runs through Seoul.
Why not the others:
(A) The Yangtze is in China.
(B) The Great Leap Forward was a failed Chinese campaign of 1958.
(D) The Meiji Restoration was nineteenth-century Japan.
Key point: South Korea became a major economy within a few decades.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: Globalisation and the state — the false claim
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Globalisation always weakens the capacity of the state and never strengthens it.
(B) Technology, such as the internet and the telegraph before it, has been a key cause of globalisation.
(C) Developed countries guard their borders, so people move less freely than goods and capital.
(D) Globalisation increases the interconnectedness of the world.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A) only
Why: Only (A) is false: NCERT notes that in some ways state capacity has increased, because states have new technology for gathering information about citizens.
Why not the others: (B) technology is a central cause. (C) visa and immigration controls limit the movement of people. (D) interconnectedness is what globalisation means. Options (B), (C) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Globalisation reshapes the state rather than simply shrinking it.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: Arms-control agreements and what they do
questions.question:
Match List-I (Agreement) with List-II (Purpose).

List-I
(A) Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty (1972)
(B) Chemical Weapons Convention
(C) Non-Proliferation Treaty
(D) Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty

List-II
(I) Cuts in the long-range nuclear arsenals of the US and the USSR
(II) Lets only the countries that tested nuclear weapons before 1967 keep them
(III) Stops the US and the USSR from using missile defences as a basis for nuclear war
(IV) Bans the production and possession of chemical weapons
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: The ABM Treaty limited missile defence systems (III). The CWC bans chemical weapons (IV). The NPT lets only states that tested before 1967 keep nuclear weapons (II). START cut strategic arsenals (I).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps the ABM Treaty and the CWC. Option (C) swaps the CWC and the NPT. Option (D) swaps the NPT and START.
Key point: Arms control regulates weapons; disarmament abolishes them.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Democratic Upsurge and Coalition Politics
questions.sub_topic: Outside support for the first UPA government
questions.question: The first UPA government (2004) depended for its majority on the outside support of:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) the Left parties
Why: The Left parties supported the UPA from outside without joining the government.
Why not the others:
(A) The BJP led the opposition NDA.
(B) The Shiv Sena was part of the NDA.
(D) The Telugu Desam Party had supported the NDA.
Key point: Outside support was a common feature of coalition governments.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: The Congress split and its aftermath — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) In 1969 the Congress split into the Congress (O) and the Congress (R).
(B) Indira Gandhi's government abolished the privy purses of former princes.
(C) The split arose partly from the contest over the 1969 presidential election.
(D) The Congress (R) won the 1971 election with only a narrow majority.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) the party split into the Congress (O), for "Organisation", and the Congress (R), for "Requisitionists". (B) privy purses were abolished by a constitutional amendment in 1971. (C) the clash over the presidential election of 1969 was a key cause.
Why not the others: (D) is false: Indira Gandhi's Congress (R) won 352 seats, a two-thirds majority. Options (B) and (D) include (D); option (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: The split ended in a decisive victory for Indira Gandhi in 1971.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: Why the USSR collapsed and who led it — the false claim
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The Soviet economy was planned and controlled by the state.
(B) The intervention in Afghanistan in 1979 weakened the Soviet system.
(C) Boris Yeltsin was President of the Soviet Union when it broke up in 1991.
(D) The rise of nationalism in republics such as the Baltic states and Ukraine contributed to the collapse.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C) only
Why: Only (C) is false: Gorbachev was President of the Soviet Union. Yeltsin was President of Russia, and led the move to dissolve the USSR.
Why not the others: (A) the Soviet state owned and planned the economy. (B) the Afghan war drained the system. (D) nationalist demands in the republics hastened the break-up. Options (A), (B) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Gorbachev headed the USSR; Yeltsin headed Russia.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: The most important cause of globalisation
questions.question: According to NCERT, the most important cause of globalisation is:
options: A) the end of colonial empires
B) the spread of a single world language
C) the abolition of all national borders
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) technology
Why: Technology, from the telegraph and telephone to the microchip and the internet, has made it possible for ideas, capital, commodities and people to move rapidly.
Why not the others:
(A) Decolonisation is not named as the main cause.
(B) There is no single world language.
(C) Borders still exist.
Key point: Technology underpins every flow of globalisation.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: Which is NOT a component of India's security strategy
questions.question: India's security strategy has four broad components. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
options: A) Joining a military bloc led by a superpower
C) Strengthening international norms and institutions
D) Developing its economy to reduce poverty and inequality
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Joining a military bloc led by a superpower
Why: India has relied on its own strength, international norms, internal security and economic development; joining a superpower's military bloc is not part of its strategy.
Why not the others:
(B) Military capability is the first component.
(C) International norms and institutions are the second.
(D) Economic development is the fourth; internal security is the third.
Key point: Non-alignment shaped India's security strategy.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: Central Asian republic that went through a civil war till 2001
questions.question: Which Central Asian republic went through a civil war that lasted about ten years, until 2001?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Tajikistan
Why: Tajikistan went through a civil war that lasted about a decade, until 2001.
Why not the others:
(A) Kazakhstan has had a stable government.
(B) Uzbekistan has had a strongly centralised government.
(C) Turkmenistan has had a closed but stable government.
Key point: The region also has big hydrocarbon resources, which draw outside powers.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: UN Secretaries-General and their countries
questions.question:
Match List-I (Secretary-General) with List-II (Country).

List-I
(A) Trygve Lie
(B) Dag Hammarskjöld
(C) U Thant
(D) Ban Ki-moon

List-II
(I) Sweden
(II) Norway
(III) South Korea
(IV) Myanmar (Burma)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III)
Why: Trygve Lie of Norway was the first Secretary-General (II). Dag Hammarskjöld was from Sweden (I). U Thant was from Burma, now Myanmar (IV). Ban Ki-moon is from South Korea (III).
Why not the others: Option (B) swaps the two Scandinavians. Option (C) swaps U Thant and Ban Ki-moon. Option (D) puts Hammarskjöld in Myanmar.
Key point: Secretaries-General come from many regions, not from the permanent five.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Recent Issues and Challenges
questions.sub_topic: Figures in recent Indian politics
questions.question:
Match List-I (Person) with List-II (Association).

List-I
(A) Kanshi Ram
(B) Manmohan Singh
(C) Mayawati
(D) L.K. Advani

List-II
(I) Led the rath yatra of 1990
(II) Finance Minister who launched the 1991 reforms
(III) Became Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh as a BSP leader
(IV) Founded the Bahujan Samaj Party
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(IV), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(I)
Why: Kanshi Ram founded the BSP in 1984 (IV). Manmohan Singh, as Finance Minister, launched the 1991 reforms (II). Mayawati became Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh (III). Advani led the BJP's rath yatra in 1990 (I).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps Kanshi Ram and Mayawati. Option (B) swaps Manmohan Singh and Advani. Option (C) swaps Mayawati and Advani.
Key point: Dalit politics, reforms and the Ayodhya issue shaped the 1990s.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: Words and events of the Emergency period
questions.question:
Match List-I (Term) with List-II (Meaning).

List-I
(A) 42nd Amendment
(B) Turkman Gate
(C) Compulsory sterilisation
(D) Committed bureaucracy

List-II
(I) Forced demolition of houses in Delhi
(II) Officials expected to be loyal to the ruling party's policies
(III) Extended the term of the Lok Sabha from five to six years
(IV) Coercive excess in the family-planning drive
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Why: The 42nd Amendment made many changes, including a six-year term for the Lok Sabha (III). Houses were forcibly demolished at Turkman Gate in Delhi (I). Compulsory sterilisation was the worst excess of the family-planning drive (IV). A committed bureaucracy meant officials loyal to the ruling party (II).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps the amendment and Turkman Gate. Option (C) swaps Turkman Gate and sterilisation. Option (D) swaps sterilisation and the committed bureaucracy.
Key point: The Shah Commission later documented such excesses.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: Congress President who expelled Indira Gandhi in 1969
questions.question: Which Congress President expelled Indira Gandhi from the party in November 1969?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) S. Nijalingappa
Why: S. Nijalingappa, then Congress President, expelled Indira Gandhi. The party then split into two.
Why not the others:
(A) Kamaraj had been Congress President earlier, from 1964.
(B) Morarji Desai was a Syndicate ally and Deputy Prime Minister.
(C) Sanjeeva Reddy was the defeated presidential candidate.
Key point: The expulsion formalised the 1969 split.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: Patent issue that sparked resistance in India
questions.question: In India, resistance to globalisation included protests against attempts by American and European firms to patent plants such as:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) neem
Why: There was resistance to the patenting of plants such as neem by foreign firms, along with protests by left-wing groups and trade unions.
Why not the others: (A), (C), (D) The patent controversy NCERT notes concerned plants such as neem, not tea, jute or cotton.
Key point: Resistance in India targeted both economic and cultural effects.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Politics of Planned Development
questions.sub_topic: People associated with India's development debates
questions.question:
Match List-I (Person) with List-II (Association).

List-I
(A) P.C. Mahalanobis
(B) J.C. Kumarappa
(C) Verghese Kurien
(D) K.N. Raj

List-II
(I) Operation Flood and the Anand cooperative movement
(II) Drafted the Second Five Year Plan, with its stress on heavy industry
(III) Young economist who argued for a slower pace in the first plan
(IV) Gandhian economist who worked out an alternative to the dominant model
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Why: Mahalanobis drafted the Second Plan (II). Kumarappa offered a Gandhian alternative, with a stress on rural industry (IV). Kurien led the cooperative dairy movement and Operation Flood (I). K.N. Raj argued that India should "hasten slowly" in its early plans (III).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps Mahalanobis and Kumarappa. Option (B) gives Operation Flood to Kumarappa. Option (D) swaps Kurien and K.N. Raj.
Key point: The planning debate included both state-led and Gandhian voices.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Democratic Upsurge and Coalition Politics
questions.sub_topic: Event during the 1991 election campaign
questions.question: Which event took place during the campaign for the 1991 Lok Sabha election?
options: A) The assassination of Rajiv Gandhi
B) The assassination of Indira Gandhi
C) The declaration of the Emergency
D) The formation of the BJP
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The assassination of Rajiv Gandhi
Why: Rajiv Gandhi was assassinated in May 1991 while campaigning in Tamil Nadu.
Why not the others:
(B) Indira Gandhi was assassinated in 1984.
(C) The Emergency was declared in 1975.
(D) The BJP was formed in 1980.
Key point: The Congress formed a government after the 1991 election under Rao.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: Outcomes of global environmental politics
questions.question:
Match List-I (Agreement or body) with List-II (Description).

List-I
(A) Agenda 21
(B) UNFCCC
(C) Kyoto Protocol
(D) World Council of Indigenous Peoples

List-II
(I) Set emission targets for industrialised countries
(II) Formed in 1975 to represent indigenous peoples
(III) The 1992 framework convention on climate change
(IV) A list of development practices recommended at Rio
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: Agenda 21 listed development practices adopted at Rio (IV). The UNFCCC was the 1992 framework convention on climate change (III). The Kyoto Protocol set targets for industrialised countries (I). The WCIP was formed in 1975 (II).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps Agenda 21 and the UNFCCC. Option (B) swaps the UNFCCC and Kyoto. Option (D) swaps Kyoto and the WCIP.
Key point: Rio produced Agenda 21 and the UNFCCC; Kyoto came under the UNFCCC.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: Bangladesh's place in India's eastern policy
questions.question: Bangladesh is important to India mainly because it is part of India's:
options: A) Look West policy towards the countries of the Gulf
B) membership of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation
C) Look East policy, linking India to South-East Asia
D) long-term plan to seek links with the European Union
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Look East policy, linking India to South-East Asia
Why: Bangladesh is part of India's Look East (Act East) policy, which seeks to link India with South-East Asia through Myanmar.
Why not the others:
(A) Look West concerns the Gulf.
(B) Bangladesh is not an SCO member.
(D) India is not seeking EU membership.
Key point: Geography makes Bangladesh key to India's eastern links.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: Milestones of India's external relations in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
(A) India's second set of nuclear tests at Pokhran
(B) The Chinese attack on India
(C) The Kargil conflict
(D) The Bandung conference
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (D), (B), (A), (C)
Why: (D) The Bandung conference was held in 1955. (B) China attacked in October 1962. (A) India tested again at Pokhran in May 1998. (C) The Kargil conflict took place in 1999.
Why not the others: Option (B) puts 1962 before Bandung. Option (C) puts Kargil before the 1998 tests. Option (D) puts the 1998 tests before 1962.
Key point: 1955 → 1962 → 1998 → 1999.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: Country that broke up into several provinces after 1991
questions.question: Which Balkan country broke up into several new states, among them Bosnia and Herzegovina, Slovenia and Croatia, amid armed conflict after the end of the Cold War?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Yugoslavia
Why: Yugoslavia broke apart in the 1990s. Several provinces, including Slovenia, Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, declared independence.
Why not the others:
(B) Bulgaria did not break up.
(C) Romania did not break up.
(D) Czechoslovakia split peacefully into two states, not several amid war.
Key point: The break-up of Yugoslavia was the most violent in post-communist Europe.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: Origin of the Socialist Party
questions.question: Fill in the blank: The Socialist Party traced its roots to the ________, formed in 1934 within the Indian National Congress.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Congress Socialist Party
Why: The Congress Socialist Party was formed in 1934 by young leaders within the Congress who wanted a more radical, egalitarian Congress. Its members later formed the Socialist Party.
Why not the others:
(A) The Forward Bloc was founded by Subhas Chandra Bose in 1939.
(C) The Swaraj Party was formed in 1923 by C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru.
(D) The Kisan Mazdoor Praja Party was formed after Independence.
Key point: The Socialists began as a group inside the Congress.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: Order of China's privatisation steps
questions.question: In China's economic reforms, agriculture was privatised first, followed by industry. In which years did these happen?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Agriculture in 1982, industry in 1998
Why: China privatised agriculture in 1982 and industry in 1998. It also lowered trade barriers and set up SEZs.
Why not the others:
(B) 1949 was the Communist revolution; 1978 began the reforms.
(C) 2001 is when China joined the WTO.
(D) This reverses the two steps.
Key point: China reformed farming first, then industry.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: 1972 report that warned about the planet's resources
questions.question: In 1972 the Club of Rome published a book that warned about the depletion of the Earth's resources against a growing world population. It was called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Limits to Growth
Why: The Club of Rome's Limits to Growth (1972) dramatised the risk of resource depletion.
Why not the others:
(A) Our Common Future was the Brundtland Report of 1987.
(C) Silent Spring was Rachel Carson's 1962 book on pesticides.
(D) Agenda 21 came from Rio in 1992.
Key point: Environmental concern entered global politics in the 1970s.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: Criterion NOT proposed for new permanent members
questions.question: Several criteria have been proposed for new permanent members of the Security Council. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
options: A) Being a major economic power
B) Being a substantial contributor to the UN budget
C) Never having fought a war with a neighbour
D) Respecting democracy and human rights
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Never having fought a war with a neighbour
Why: The proposed criteria include being a major economic power, a major military power, a substantial contributor to the UN budget, and a big nation in population. A new member should also respect democracy and human rights, and make the Council more representative. Never having fought a war is not one of them.
Why not the others: (A), (B), (D) are among the proposed criteria.
Key point: India argues it meets most of these criteria.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: Bangladesh and Sri Lanka since independence — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Bangladesh was part of Pakistan from 1947 to 1971.
(B) Sri Lanka has kept a democratic political system since independence in 1948.
(C) In 1975 Bangladesh's constitution was amended to a presidential form, with only one party allowed.
(D) Sri Lanka's ethnic conflict was mainly between the Sinhala majority and the Muslim minority.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) Bangladesh was East Pakistan until 1971. (B) Sri Lanka has stayed a democracy despite civil war. (C) in 1975 Mujib's government moved to a presidential system with a single party, the Awami League.
Why not the others: (D) is false: the conflict was between the Sinhala majority and Tamils of Indian origin, led by the LTTE. Options (C) and (D) include (D); option (B) leaves out (C).
Key point: South Asian countries took very different democratic paths.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: Year Nepal became a democratic republic
questions.question: In which year was Nepal's monarchy abolished, making it a democratic republic?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 2008
Why: Nepal's Constituent Assembly abolished the monarchy in 2008, ending centuries of royal rule.
Why not the others:
(A) In 1990 the king accepted a democratic constitution, but the monarchy continued.
(C) In 2002 the king dissolved Parliament.
(D) Nepal adopted a new constitution in 2015, but the monarchy had gone in 2008.
Key point: Monarchy ended in Nepal in 2008.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: When Article 370 ceased to apply
questions.question: The special status that Article 370 gave Jammu and Kashmir was ended in:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) August 2019
Why: In August 2019 Parliament ended the special status under Article 370 and reorganised the State into two Union Territories.
Why not the others:
(A) January 1950 is when the Constitution came into force.
(B) August 1975 falls during the Emergency.
(D) December 2004 has no connection with Article 370.
Key point: 2019 changed Jammu and Kashmir's constitutional position.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: Shared vision of India and Russia
questions.question: India and Russia share a vision of world order in which several centres of power co-exist. This is called a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) multipolar world
Why: Both countries favour a multipolar world, with collective security, regional power centres and a strong UN.
Why not the others:
(A) A unipolar world has one dominant power.
(C) Bipolarity ended with the Cold War.
(D) A stateless world is not their vision.
Key point: Multipolarity is a key idea in India–Russia ties.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: Human Rights Watch
questions.question: Human Rights Watch is:
options: A) an international NGO, the largest of its kind in the US
B) the human rights wing of the UN Security Council
C) an international court that tries war criminals
D) an agency of the World Bank that monitors loans
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) an international NGO, the largest of its kind in the US
Why: Human Rights Watch is an international NGO that researches and advocates on human rights; it is the largest such organisation in the US.
Why not the others:
(B) The Security Council has no such wing.
(C) Courts such as the International Criminal Court try war crimes.
(D) It has no link with the World Bank.
Key point: NGOs like Amnesty and HRW draw attention to human rights abuses.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: South Asian country with high human development despite conflict
questions.question: Which South Asian country has achieved high levels of human development and was among the first developing countries to control population growth, despite a long ethnic conflict?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Sri Lanka
Why: Sri Lanka has recorded good economic growth and high human development indicators, despite its long ethnic conflict.
Why not the others:
(A) Pakistan has lower human development indicators.
(B) Nepal has lower human development indicators.
(C) Afghanistan has suffered prolonged war and low human development.
Key point: Sri Lanka stands out in South Asia for human development.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: How many princely states existed at Independence
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

At Independence, British India contained more than five hundred princely states, each ruled by a prince who had accepted British paramountcy. When paramountcy lapsed in 1947, these rulers became legally free to join India or Pakistan, or to remain independent. The interim government took a firm but flexible line. Three considerations guided it: most people in the princely states clearly wanted to be part of India; the government was willing to give some regions a measure of autonomy; and, coming after Partition, the unity of the country's territory had become supremely important. Through persuasion, almost every ruler signed a document by which his state agreed to become part of India. A few cases proved harder. The Nizam of Hyderabad wanted independence and signed only a temporary arrangement with India while a people's movement grew against him; in September 1948 the Indian Army moved in and the state was integrated. In Manipur the Maharaja held elections to an assembly on the basis of universal adult franchise, but in September 1949 the Government of India pressed him to sign a merger agreement without consulting that popularly elected assembly, which caused lasting resentment.

Question: The passage refers to "more than five hundred princely states". About how many were there?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 565
Why: NCERT puts the number of princely states at 565. They covered about one-third of the land area of British India.
Why not the others: (A), (B), (D) 125, 330 and 1100 are not the figures NCERT gives.
Key point: About 565 states had to be brought into the Union.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: Document by which princely states joined India
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

When paramountcy lapsed in 1947, these rulers became legally free to join India or Pakistan, or to remain independent. The interim government took a firm but flexible line. In Manipur the Maharaja held elections to an assembly on the basis of universal adult franchise, but in September 1949 the Government of India pressed him to sign a merger agreement without consulting that popularly elected assembly, which caused lasting resentment.

Question: The passage says almost every ruler signed "a document by which his state agreed to become part of India". This document was called the:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Instrument of Accession
Why: Rulers signed the Instrument of Accession, agreeing that their state would become part of India.
Why not the others:
(B) A Standstill Agreement was a temporary arrangement, like the Nizam's.
(C) The Objectives Resolution was moved in the Constituent Assembly.
(D) There was no "Merger Ordinance".
Key point: The Instrument of Accession brought most princely states in peacefully.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: When Hyderabad was integrated
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

At Independence, British India contained more than five hundred princely states, each ruled by a prince who had accepted British paramountcy. When paramountcy lapsed in 1947, these rulers became legally free to join India or Pakistan, or to remain independent. The interim government took a firm but flexible line. Three considerations guided it: most people in the princely states clearly wanted to be part of India; the government was willing to give some regions a measure of autonomy; and, coming after Partition, the unity of the country's territory had become supremely important. Through persuasion, almost every ruler signed a document by which his state agreed to become part of India. A few cases proved harder. The Nizam of Hyderabad wanted independence and signed only a temporary arrangement with India while a people's movement grew against him; in September 1948 the Indian Army moved in and the state was integrated. In Manipur the Maharaja held elections to an assembly on the basis of universal adult franchise, but in September 1949 the Government of India pressed him to sign a merger agreement without consulting that popularly elected assembly, which caused lasting resentment.

Question: According to the passage, when was Hyderabad integrated into India after the Indian Army moved in?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) September 1948
Why: After months of a standstill arrangement and a growing people's movement, the Indian Army moved against the Nizam's forces in September 1948. The Nizam surrendered and Hyderabad became part of India.
Why not the others:
(A) August 1947 was Independence, when Hyderabad had not joined.
(C) January 1950 is when the Constitution came into force.
(D) November 1956 is when the States Reorganisation Act took effect.
Key point: Hyderabad joined after army action in 1948.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: Why Manipur's merger caused resentment
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

At Independence, British India contained more than five hundred princely states, each ruled by a prince who had accepted British paramountcy. When paramountcy lapsed in 1947, these rulers became legally free to join India or Pakistan, or to remain independent. The interim government took a firm but flexible line. Three considerations guided it: most people in the princely states clearly wanted to be part of India; the government was willing to give some regions a measure of autonomy; and, coming after Partition, the unity of the country's territory had become supremely important. Through persuasion, almost every ruler signed a document by which his state agreed to become part of India. A few cases proved harder. The Nizam of Hyderabad wanted independence and signed only a temporary arrangement with India while a people's movement grew against him; in September 1948 the Indian Army moved in and the state was integrated. In Manipur the Maharaja held elections to an assembly on the basis of universal adult franchise, but in September 1949 the Government of India pressed him to sign a merger agreement without consulting that popularly elected assembly, which caused lasting resentment.

Question: Based on the passage, why did the merger of Manipur with India cause lasting resentment?
options: A) The Maharaja refused to hold any elections to an assembly in Manipur.
B) Manipur was made a part of Pakistan for two years after Independence.
C) The Indian Army fought a long war against the forces of the Maharaja.
D) The merger was signed without consulting the elected assembly.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The merger was signed without consulting the elected assembly.
Why: Manipur had an elected assembly, chosen by universal adult franchise. The merger agreement of September 1949 was signed under pressure without consulting it, which left resentment that persists.
Why not the others:
(A) The Maharaja did hold elections, in 1948.
(B) Manipur was never part of Pakistan.
(C) There was no war; the issue was the way the merger was done.
Key point: The process of integration mattered, not only its result.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: Considerations behind the government's approach to the princely states
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

At Independence, British India contained more than five hundred princely states, each ruled by a prince who had accepted British paramountcy. When paramountcy lapsed in 1947, these rulers became legally free to join India or Pakistan, or to remain independent. The interim government took a firm but flexible line. Three considerations guided it: most people in the princely states clearly wanted to be part of India; the government was willing to give some regions a measure of autonomy; and, coming after Partition, the unity of the country's territory had become supremely important. Through persuasion, almost every ruler signed a document by which his state agreed to become part of India. A few cases proved harder. The Nizam of Hyderabad wanted independence and signed only a temporary arrangement with India while a people's movement grew against him; in September 1948 the Indian Army moved in and the state was integrated. In Manipur the Maharaja held elections to an assembly on the basis of universal adult franchise, but in September 1949 the Government of India pressed him to sign a merger agreement without consulting that popularly elected assembly, which caused lasting resentment.

Question: Which of the following was NOT one of the considerations that, according to the passage, guided the government's approach to the princely states?
options: A) Most people in the princely states wanted to be part of India.
B) The government was willing to grant some regions autonomy.
C) Princes were to keep paramountcy over their states after 1947.
D) After Partition, the unity of India's territory had become very important.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Princes were to keep paramountcy over their states after 1947.
Why: Paramountcy lapsed in 1947; the government did not seek to give it back to the princes. The other three are the considerations the passage lists.
Why not the others:
(A) The people's wish to join India is the first consideration.
(B) Flexibility over autonomy is the second.
(D) Territorial unity after Partition is the third.
Key point: Firmness with flexibility, guided by the people's wishes.
